title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 159 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 781–783 (Night 159, continuing directly from nights-158), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 159 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. Abū al-Ḥasan goes back to his shop with a heavy heart; the next day ʿAlī pours out his love to him in two short poems. Fearing that the affair will come out and ruin him, Abū al-Ḥasan tells a friend he means to settle his affairs and leave for Basra, and goes. The friend, finding him gone, calls on ʿAlī, who is shaken by the news and sends his servant to Abū al-Ḥasan's house; the servant comes back with a slave-girl bearing a message from Shams al-Nahār. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-ninth night,
sentences.n: al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-. The alif of المائة is not pronounced: the word is miʾa, and its hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ وَدَّعَ الْجَارِيَةَ وَذَهَبَ إِلَى دُكَّانِهِ وَفَتَحَهَا وَجَلَسَ مِثْلَ عَادَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Abā al-Ḥasani waddaʿa al-jāriyata wa-dhahaba ilā dukkānihi wa-fataḥahā wa-jalasa mithla ʿādatihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan bade-farewell-to the slave-girl, and went to his-shop, and opened-it, and sat like his-habit.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan said goodbye to the slave-girl, went to his shop, opened it, and sat there as he always did.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the thread with the very words that closed Night 158. The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان); the spacing is kept. Abā al-Ḥasani is accusative after anna. fataḥahā, “he opened it”: dukkān, “shop”, is again treated as feminine. mithla ʿādatihi, “like his habit”, is an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَقَرَّ فِي مَكَانِهِ وَجَدَ قَلْبَهُ قَدِ انْقَبَضَ وَضَاقَ صَدْرُةُ وَحَارَفِي أَمْرِةِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ فِي فِكْرٍ بَقِيَّةَ يَوْمِهِ وَلَيْلَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istaqarra fī makānihi wajada qalbahu qadi inqabaḍa wa-ḍāqa ṣadruhu wa-ḥāra fī amrihi wa-lam yazal fī fikrin baqiyyata yawmihi wa-laylatihi
sentences.l: And when he-settled in his-place, he-found his-heart had contracted, and his-breast grew-narrow, and he-was-perplexed in his-affair; and he-did-not cease (to be) in thought the rest of his-day and his-night.
sentences.i: But once he had settled in his place, he found his heart heavy and his spirits low; he was at a loss what to do, and he stayed lost in thought for the rest of that day and all the night.
sentences.n: istaqarra, “to settle, come to rest” (Form X of qarra). wajada qalbahu qad inqabaḍa, “he found his heart had contracted”: wajada takes an object and a clause describing it. inqabaḍa (Form VII of qabaḍa), “to be gripped, shrink”, and ḍāqa ṣadruhu, “his breast grew narrow”, are both the Arabic for gloom and anxiety, the opposite of a breast “opened” in joy. The print spells the pronoun with ة twice, in صدرة (ṣadruhu) and امرة (amrihi), its habit. It also runs ḥāra and fī together (وحارفي); the spacing is kept. ḥāra fī amrihi, “he was perplexed in his affair”: he did not know what to do. lam yazal fī fikrin, “he did not cease to be in thought”: lam yazal is “to go on, remain”. baqiyyata yawmihi, “the rest of his day”, is an accusative of time.

sentences.t: وَفِى الْيَوْمِ الثَّانِي ذَهَبَ إِلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَجَلَسَ عِنْدَةُ حَتَّى ذَهَبَ النَّاسُ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī al-yawmi al-thānī dhahaba ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-jalasa ʿindahu ḥattā dhahaba al-nāsu wa-saʾalahu ʿan ḥālihi
sentences.l: And on the second day he-went to ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and sat with-him until the people went, and asked-him about his-state.
sentences.i: The next day he went to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and sat with him until the visitors had left, and then asked him how he was.
sentences.n: The print writes fī as فى and spells the pronoun of ʿindahu, “with him”, with ة (عندة). al-yawm al-thānī, “the second day”, is “the next day”. al-nās, “the people”, are the visitors who came to sit with the sick man; Abū al-Ḥasan waits until he and ʿAlī are alone. The hamza of سأله is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ فِي شَكْوَي الْغَرَامِ وَمَابِهِ مِنَ الْوَجْدِ وَالْهُيَامِ وَأَنْشَدَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha fī shakwā al-gharāmi wa-mā bihi mina al-wajdi wa-al-huyāmi wa-anshada qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And he-began in complaint of the passion and what (was) in-him of the ardour and the love-madness, and he-recited the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: ʿAlī began to complain of his passion and of all the longing and love-sickness he suffered, and he recited the poet's words:
sentences.n: akhadha fī, “to take to, begin” something. The print writes shakwā, “complaint”, with a final ي (شكوي), its usual swapping of ي and ى; it is pointed شَكْوَي and read shakwā. It also runs mā bihi, “what was in him”, together (ومابه); the spacing is kept. huyām is love that drives one wild, like the thirst that sends a camel wandering; gharām and huyām rhyme.

sentences.t:
شَكَى اَلَمَ اْلغَرَامِ النَّاسُ قَبْلِيْ * وَرَوَّعَ بِالنَّوى حَيٌّ وَمَيْتُ
وَاَمَّا مِثْلُ مَا ضَمَّتْ ضُلُوْعِيْ * فَاِنِّيْ لَا سَمِعْتُ وَلَا رَأَيْتُ
sentences.tr:
shakā alama al-gharāmi al-nāsu qablī * wa-rawwaʿa bi-al-nawā ḥayyun wa-maytu
wa-ammā mithlu mā ḍammat ḍulūʿī * fa-innī lā samiʿtu wa-lā raʾaytu
sentences.l:
People complained of the pain of passion before-me, * and with parting living and dead have-struck-terror;
but as for the like of what my-ribs have-enclosed, * I neither heard nor saw (it).
sentences.i:
Others before me have cried out at love's pain, and parting has brought dread on the living and the dead;
but the like of what my ribs enclose I have never heard of, and never seen.
sentences.n: Metre: wāfir. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَلَمَ, وَاَمَّا and فَاِنِّيْ, where the edition marks no hamza, the sukūn it sets on long vowels (قَبْلِيْ, ضُلُوْعِيْ), and its odd pointing of the article in اْلغَرَامِ, with the sukūn on the alif and a fatḥa on the lām; the hamza of رَأَيْتُ is its own too. shakā, “he complained”, is spelt with ى, and its subject, al-nās, “people”, comes after its object. The print points rawwaʿa, “he frightened” (Form II), as active, which leaves it without an object: the sense is that parting has struck dread into living and dead alike, as if it were passive, ruwwiʿa. nawā is “distance, separation”. maytu, “dead”, is mayyit shortened, with the damma of the rhyme. ḍulūʿ, “ribs”, plural of ḍilʿ: what the ribs enclose is the heart and its pain. lā samiʿtu wa-lā raʾaytu: lā with the perfect, repeated, is “neither … nor”.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: And these lines of the poet:
sentences.n: wa-qawla is a second object of anshada, “he recited”, so it is accusative: he recited this poem too.

sentences.t:
وَلَقِيتُ مِنْ حُبِّيكَ مَالَمْ يَلْقَهُ * فِي حُبِّ لُبْنَى قَيْسُهَا الْمَجْنُونُ
لكنَّني لَمْ اَتَّبِعْ وَحْشَ الْفَلَا * كَفَعَالُ قَيْسٍ وَالْجُنُونُ فُنُونُ
sentences.tr:
wa-laqītu min ḥubbīka mā lam yalqahu * fī ḥubbi Lubnā Qaysuhā al-majnūnu
lākinnanī lam attabiʿ waḥsha al-falā * ka-faʿālu Qaysin wa-al-junūnu funūnu
sentences.l:
And I-have-met, from loving-you, what (he) did-not meet, * in the love of Lubnā, her-Qays the mad-one;
but I did-not follow the wild-beasts of the desert * like the doing of Qays; and madness (has) kinds.
sentences.i:
Loving you, I have suffered what Qays the madman never suffered for love of Lubnā;
but I have not run off after the wild beasts of the waste as Qays did: madness comes in many kinds.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَتَّبِعْ, where the edition marks no hamza, and لكنَّني, where it sets only the shadda. The print runs mā lam (مَالَمْ) together; the spacing is kept. ḥubbīka, “my love of you”, is ḥubbika with the vowel lengthened, which the metre needs; it may also be read as ḥubbī, “my love”, with -ka, “you”, added, a loose double pronoun. Qaysuhā, “her Qays”: Lubnā's Qays is Qays ibn Dharīḥ, but the poem gives him the name al-Majnūn, “the madman”, which belongs to the Qays who loved Laylā and went to live among the wild beasts of the desert; the two lovers were confused often enough. After ka-, “like”, faʿāl, “doing, deed”, should be genitive, faʿāli; the print points it with a damma, kept here. al-junūnu funūnu, “madness is of kinds”, closes the poem with a proverb-like turn.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ أَنَا مَا رَأَيْتُ وَلَاسَمِعْتُ بِمِثْلِكَ فِي مَحَبَّتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani anā mā raʾaytu wa-lā samiʿtu bi-mithlika fī maḥabbatika
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: I, I-have-not seen nor heard of the-like-of-you in your-love.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “I have never seen or heard of anyone like you in love.
sentences.n: Abū al-Ḥasan picks up the poem's last words, “I neither heard nor saw”, and turns them on ʿAlī. The print runs lā and samiʿtu together (ولاسمعت); the spacing is kept. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”: the verb chooses bi- for what one hears about. The bare alif of رايت carries no hamza in the print; it is supplied.

sentences.t: كَيْفَ يَكُونُ هَذَا الْوَجْدُ وَضَعْفُ الْحَرَكَةِ وَقَدْ تَعَلَّقْتَ بِحَبِيبٍ مُوَافِقٍ
sentences.tr: kayfa yakūnu hādhā al-wajdu wa-ḍaʿfu al-ḥarakati wa-qad taʿallaqta bi-ḥabībin muwāfiqin
sentences.l: How is there this ardour and weakness of movement, and-indeed you-have-attached-yourself to a-beloved agreeing?
sentences.i: How can there be such longing, and such weakness that you can barely stir, when the one you love loves you in return?
sentences.n: kāna, with no predicate, means “to be, to come about”: “how does this ardour come about?” ḍaʿf al-ḥaraka, “weakness of movement”, is ʿAlī's sickbed state. wa-qad taʿallaqta, “when you have attached yourself”, is a circumstantial clause opened by wa-; taʿallaqa bi- (Form V), “to cling to, become attached to”, chooses bi- for what one clings to, and is the usual verb for falling in love. The shadda and the final fatḥa of تعلّقتَ are the print's own, the fatḥa marking “you”. muwāfiq, “agreeing, in accord” (Form III participle), is a beloved who returns the love.

sentences.t: فَكَيْفَ إِذَا أَحْبَبْتَ حَبِيبًا مُخَالِفًا مُخَادِعًا فَكَانَ أَمْرُكَ يَنْكَشِفُ
sentences.tr: fa-kayfa idhā aḥbabta ḥabīban mukhālifan mukhādiʿan fa-kāna amruka yankashifu
sentences.l: So how (would it be) if you-loved a-beloved contrary, deceiving? Then your-affair would-be becoming-exposed.
sentences.i: What would it be like if you loved someone who crossed you and played you false? Then everyone would know your secret.”
sentences.n: fa-kayfa idhā …, “so how (would it be) if …”, leaves the answer unsaid. mukhālif, “contrary, opposing” (Form III), and mukhādiʿ, “deceiving” (Form III), are the opposite of muwāfiq above. fa-kāna amruka yankashifu, “then your affair would come to light”: kāna with an imperfect describes what would follow; the sense is that a lover tormented by a false beloved could not keep his secret, whereas ʿAlī's luck in love should let him keep his. yankashifu, Form VII of kashafa, “to be uncovered”.

sentences.t: قَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ فَأَعْجَبَ عَلِيَّ ابْنَ بَكَّارٍ كَلَامِي وَرَكَنَ إِلَيْهِ وَشَكَرَنِي عَلَى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: qāla Abū al-Ḥasani fa-aʿjaba ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin kalāmī wa-rakana ilayhi wa-shakaranī ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: Abū al-Ḥasan said: And my-words pleased ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and he-leaned to-it, and thanked-me for that.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said: My words pleased ʿAlī ibn Bakkār; he took comfort in them and thanked me for them.
sentences.n: The tale turns again to Abū al-Ḥasan's own telling, in the first person. The print runs Abū and al-Ḥasan together (ابوالحسن); the spacing is kept. aʿjaba, “to please” (Form IV): ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin is its object, set before the subject kalāmī, “my words”. The print writes ibn with its alif (ابن) between the two names. rakana ilā, “to lean on, trust in, take comfort in”: the verb chooses ilā; -hi is kalām, “speech”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لِي صَاحِبٌ يَطَّلِعُ عَلَى أَمْرِي وَأَمْرِةِ وَيَعْلَمُ أَنَّنَا مُتَوَافِقَانِ وَلَا يَعْلَمُ أَحَدٌ مَا بَيْنَنَا غَيْرُةُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lī ṣāḥibun yaṭṭaliʿu ʿalā amrī wa-amrihi wa-yaʿlamu annanā mutawāfiqāni wa-lā yaʿlamu aḥadun mā baynanā ghayruhu
sentences.l: And there-was for-me a-friend (who) was-acquainted with my-affair and his-affair, and knew that-we (were) two-in-accord; and no-one knew what (was) between-us other-than-him.
sentences.i: Now I had a friend who knew all about my affairs and ʿAlī's, and knew that we two were close; no one but he knew what there was between us.
sentences.n: kāna lī ṣāḥibun, “there was to me a friend”: possession is said with li-, “to, for”. yaṭṭaliʿu ʿalā, “to be acquainted with, to see into” (Form VIII of ṭalaʿa), describes the indefinite ṣāḥib without a relative word. The print spells the pronoun with ة in امرة (amrihi, “his affair”, ʿAlī's) and غيرة (ghayruhu, “other than he”), its habit. mutawāfiqāni, “two in accord” (Form VI participle, dual): ʿAlī and Abū al-Ḥasan.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يَأْتِينِي فَيَسْأَلُنِي عَنْ حَالِ عَلِيِّ ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yaʾtīnī fa-yasʾalunī ʿan ḥāli ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And he-used-to come-to-me and ask-me about the state of ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: He used to come to me and ask how ʿAlī ibn Bakkār was getting on.
sentences.n: The print has يأنيني, a misprint for يأتيني, corrected here. kāna with the imperfect, kāna yaʾtīnī, “he used to come to me”, is a habit in the past. The hamzas of يأتيني and يسألني are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ قَلِيلٍ سَأَلَنِى عَنِ الْجَارِيَةِ فَخَادَعْتُهُ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ قَدْ دَعَتْهُ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda qalīlin saʾalanī ʿani al-jāriyati fa-khādaʿtuhu wa-qultu lahu qad daʿathu ilayhā
sentences.l: And after a-little he-asked-me about the slave-girl; and I-deceived-him and said to-him: She-has called-him to-her,
sentences.i: Before long he asked me about the slave-girl, and I put him off with a trick, telling him, “She has invited him to come to her,
sentences.n: The print writes the final ي of saʾalanī, “he asked me”, as ى (سألنى); its hamza is the print's own. khādaʿa, “to deceive, beguile” (Form III), the same root as mukhādiʿ above. al-jāriya here is Shams al-Nahār herself, a slave-girl of the caliph's household, not her messenger. qad daʿathu ilayhā, “she has called him to her”: what follows is the trick Abū al-Ḥasan plays on his friend.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَهَا مَا لَا مَزِيدَ عَلَيْهِ وَهَذَا آخِرُ مَا انْتَهَى مِنْ أَمْرِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna baynahu wa-baynahā mā lā mazīda ʿalayhi wa-hādhā ākhiru mā intahā min amrihimā
sentences.l: and there-was between-him and between-her what (has) no increase upon-it; and this (is) the last of what came-to-an-end of their-(two)-affair.
sentences.i: and everything that could pass between them has passed; and that is as far as their affair has gone.
sentences.n: mā lā mazīda ʿalayhi, “that to which there is no increase”, is a stock phrase for something that could go no further: lā with an accusative noun denies the whole class. baynahu wa-baynahā, “between him and between her”: Arabic repeats bayna before each pronoun. intahā, “to come to an end, reach its limit” (Form VIII of nahā). The madda of آخر is the print's own. Abū al-Ḥasan's speech to his friend runs on into the next sentence.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنِّي دَبَّرْتُ لِنَفْسِي أَمْرًا وَرَأْيًا أُرِيدُأَنْ أَعْرِضَهُ عَلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinnī dabbartu li-nafsī amran wa-raʾyan urīdu an aʿriḍahu ʿalayka
sentences.l: But I have-contrived for-myself a-matter and a-view (that) I-want to lay-it-before you.
sentences.i: But I have worked out a plan for myself, a course of action I want to put to you.”
sentences.n: Abū al-Ḥasan is still speaking to his friend, the one man who knows his part in the affair. dabbara amran, “to arrange a matter”, Form II of the root of dubur, “the back, the end”: to think a thing through to its outcome. li-nafsī, “for myself”: li- of benefit, and nafs, “self”, carries the pronoun. amran wa-raʾyan, “a matter and a view”, two words for one plan. urīdu an aʿriḍahu has no relative word: a clause describing the indefinite raʾyan, “a view I want to lay before you”. The print runs urīdu and an together (اريدان). ʿaraḍa ʿalā, “to lay before, put to”: ʿalā marks the one asked to judge. The hamza of ورأيا is the print's own; the others are supplied.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صَاحِبُهُ مَا هُوَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ṣāḥibuhu mā huwa
sentences.l: And his-companion said to-him: What (is) it?
sentences.i: His friend said, “What is it?”
sentences.n: mā huwa, “what is it?”: huwa, “he, it”, is masculine because it points back to amr and raʾy. ṣāḥib, “companion, friend”, with -hu, “his”.

sentences.t: قَالَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ اعْلَمْ يَا أَخِي أَنِّي رَجُلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ بِكَثْرَةِ الْمُعَامَلَاتِ بَيْنَ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ وَأَخْشَى يَا أَخِي أَنْ يَنْكَشِفَ أَمْرُهُمَا فَيَكُونَ ذَلِكَ سَبَبًا لِهَلَاكِي وَأَخْذِ مَالِي وَهَتْكِ عِرْضِي وَعِرْضِ عِيَالِي
sentences.tr: qāla Abū al-Ḥasani iʿlam yā akhī annī rajulun maʿrūfun bi-kathrati al-muʿāmalāti bayna al-rijāli wa-al-nisāʾi wa-akhshā yā akhī an yankashifa amruhumā fa-yakūna dhālika sababan li-halākī wa-akhdhi mālī wa-hatki ʿirḍī wa-ʿirḍi ʿiyālī
sentences.l: Abū al-Ḥasan said: Know, O my-brother, that I (am) a-man known for the-muchness of the dealings between the men and the women; and I-fear, O my-brother, that their-affair be-uncovered, and that-be a-cause for my-ruin, and the taking of my-wealth, and the tearing of my-honour and the honour of my-household.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said, “You should know, my brother, that I am a man known for doing a great deal of business with men and women alike, and I am afraid, my brother, that their affair will come to light, and that this will be my ruin: my goods taken, my honour torn open, and the honour of my family with it.
sentences.n: ابوالحسن is printed as one word again. iʿlam, “know!”, opens a statement the speaker wants taken to heart; its alif is a joining alif, with no hamza. muʿāmalāt, “dealings, transactions” (Form III of ʿamila): he is a merchant whose trade takes in women as well as men, so he is widely known and talk about him would spread. -humā, “the two of them”, is ʿAlī and Shams al-Nahār. fa-yakūna is subjunctive, still governed by an: “that it be uncovered and that it be”. sababan li-, “a cause for”: li- marks what is caused. hatk, “tearing a veil”, of honour is disgrace made public; ʿirḍ is the honour of a man and of his women, and ʿiyāl, “dependants”, here his wife and children.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اقْتَضَى رَأْيِي أَنْ أَجْمَعَ مَالِي وَأُجَهِّزَ حَالِي وَأَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ الْبَصْرَةِ وَأُقِيمَ بِهَا حَتَّى أَنْظُرَ مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمَا بِحَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُ بِي أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi iqtaḍā raʾyī an ajmaʿa mālī wa-ujahhiza ḥālī wa-atawajjaha ilā madīnati al-Baṣrati wa-uqīma bihā ḥattā anẓura mā yakūnu min amrihimā bi-ḥaythu lā yashʿuru bī aḥadun
sentences.l: And my-view has-required that I-gather my-wealth and make-ready my-state, and turn-towards the city of Basra and stay in-it until I-see what will-be of their-affair, in-such-wise-that not will-be-aware of-me anyone.
sentences.i: So I have decided to gather up my goods, get myself ready, and set out for the city of Basra, and stay there until I see what comes of their affair, so that no one will know where I am.
sentences.n: iqtaḍā raʾyī, “my judgement required”, is the usual way of saying “I decided”; iqtaḍā is Form VIII of qaḍā. qad takes a linking -i before the joining alif. ajmaʿa mālī wa-ujahhiza ḥālī, “gather my goods and ready my state”, a small rhyme. jahhaza, “to equip, make ready” (Form II); the shadda on its hāʾ is the print's own, as is the one on atawajjaha, “to turn oneself towards, set out for” (Form V). aqāma bi-, “to stay in”: bi- marks the place. bi-ḥaythu, “in such a way that”: bi- + ḥaythu, “where”. shaʿara bi-, “to be aware of”: the verb chooses bi-. The hamza of رأيي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ تَمَكَّنَتِ الْمَحَبَّةُ مِنْهُمَا وَدَارَتِ الْمُرَاسَلَةُ بَيْنَهُمَا وَالْحَالُ أَنَّ الْمَاشِيَ بَيْنَهُمَا جَارِيَةٌ وَهِيَ كَاتِمَةٌ لِأَسْرَارِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qad tamakkanati al-maḥabbatu minhumā wa-dārati al-murāsalatu baynahumā wa-al-ḥālu anna al-māshiya baynahumā jāriyatun wa-hiya kātimatun li-asrārihimā
sentences.l: For the love has-taken-firm-hold of-them both, and the correspondence has-circulated between-them; and the state (is) that the go-between between-them (is) a-slave-girl, and she (is) keeping-hidden their-secrets.
sentences.i: For love has taken firm hold of them both, and letters are passing back and forth between them; and as things stand, the one who goes between them is a slave-girl, who is keeping their secrets for now.
sentences.n: tamakkana min, “to get a firm hold on” (Form V of the root of makān, “place”). murāsala, “exchanging letters” (Form III of rasala). wa-al-ḥālu anna, “and the situation is that”: a set way of bringing in the state of things. al-māshī baynahumā, “the one walking between them”, the go-between. kātimatun li-, “keeping hidden”: an active participle whose object is taken with li-, as participles often take theirs.

sentences.t: وَأَخْشَى أَنْ يَغْلِبَ عَلَيْهَا الضَّجَرُ فَتَبُوحَ بِسِرِّهِمَا لِأَحَدٍ فَيَشِيعَ خَبَرُهُمَا وَيُؤَدِّيَ ذَلِكَ إِلَى هَلَاكِي وَيَكُونَ سَبَبًا لِتَلَفِي وَلَيْسَ لِي عُذْرٌ عِنْدَ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhshā an yaghliba ʿalayhā al-ḍajaru fa-tabūḥa bi-sirrihimā li-aḥadin fa-yashīʿa khabaruhumā wa-yuʾaddiya dhālika ilā halākī wa-yakūna sababan li-talafī wa-laysa lī ʿudhrun ʿinda al-nāsi
sentences.l: And I-fear that the weariness overcome her, and she-disclose their-secret to anyone, and their-news spread, and that lead to my-ruin and be a-cause for my-destruction; and there-is-not for-me an-excuse with the people.
sentences.i: And I am afraid she will grow weary of it and let their secret out to someone, and then the story will spread, and that will lead to my ruin and be the cause of my destruction, and I will have no excuse to offer anyone.”
sentences.n: ghalaba ʿalā, “to overcome, get the better of”. ḍajar is the restlessness of someone tired of a burden: Abū al-Ḥasan fears the girl will tire of keeping quiet. bāḥa bi-, “to reveal, let out (a secret)”: the verb chooses bi- for what is revealed, and li- marks the one told; the shadda of بسرّهما is the print's own. The chain of subjunctives, fa-tabūḥa … fa-yashīʿa … wa-yuʾaddiya … wa-yakūna, all hang on an, “that”. addā ilā, “to lead to” (Form II); its hamza is the print's own. talaf, “perishing, destruction”, says again what halāk says. laysa lī ʿudhrun ʿinda al-nāsi, “I have no excuse in the eyes of people”: no one would believe he was not party to it.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صَاحِبُهُ قَدْ أَخْبَرْتَنِي بِخَبَرٍ خَطِيرٍ يَخَافُ مِنْ مِثْلِهِ الْعَاقِلُ الْخَبِيرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ṣāḥibuhu qad akhbartanī bi-khabarin khaṭīrin yakhāfu min mithlihi al-ʿāqilu al-khabīru
sentences.l: And his-companion said to-him: You-have informed-me of news grave, (that) fears from the-like-of-it the sensible, the experienced.
sentences.i: His friend said to him, “You have told me something grave, the kind of thing a man of sense and experience would fear.
sentences.n: The friend answers in rhymed prose: khaṭīr and khabīr close the two halves. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: the verb chooses bi- for the news. yakhāfu min mithlihi, “fears the like of it”: a clause describing khabarin, with no relative word; khāfa min, “to be afraid of”.

sentences.t: كَفَاكَ اللَّهُ شَرَّمَا تَخَافُهُ وَتَخْشَاهُ وَنَجَّاكَ مِمَّا تَخَافُ عُقْبَاهُ
sentences.tr: kafāka Allāhu sharra mā takhāfuhu wa-takhshāhu wa-najjāka mimmā takhāfu ʿuqbāhu
sentences.l: May-God spare-you the evil of what you-fear-it and dread-it, and may-He-rescue-you from what you-fear its-outcome.
sentences.i: God spare you the harm of what you fear and dread, and save you from whatever you fear may follow.
sentences.n: Two wishes, again rhymed: takhshāhu and ʿuqbāhu. As in shafāhu Allāhu, perfect verbs serve as a prayer, “may God …”. kafā, “to suffice”, with a person and a thing as objects, is “to spare someone something”. The print runs sharra and mā together (شرّما), and the shadda is its own, as is the one of نجّاك; najjā is Form II of najā, “to rescue”. mimmā is min + mā, “from what”. ʿuqbā, “the end, the outcome”: “what you fear its outcome” is “that whose outcome you fear”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا الرَّأْىُ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā al-raʾyu huwa al-ṣawābu
sentences.l: And this view, it (is) the right.
sentences.i: And this plan of yours is the right one.”
sentences.n: huwa, “it”, stands between subject and predicate to mark where the one ends and the other begins: “this view is the right (course)”. The print spells al-raʾy with final ى (الرأى); its hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَانْصَرَفَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَصَارَ يَقْضِي مَصَالِحَهُ وَيَتَجَهَّزُ لِلسَّفَرِ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ الْبَصْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-inṣarafa Abū al-Ḥasani ilā manzilihi wa-ṣāra yaqḍī maṣāliḥahu wa-yatajahhazu li-al-safari ilā madīnati al-Baṣrati
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan went-away to his-dwelling, and began settling his-affairs and making-himself-ready for the journey to the city of Basra.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan went home and set about settling his affairs and making ready for the journey to Basra.
sentences.n: ṣāra yaqḍī, “he became settling”: ṣāra with an imperfect verb is “he began to, set about”, a construction the Nights uses constantly. qaḍā maṣāliḥahu, “to settle one's affairs, see to one's business”; maṣāliḥ is the plural of maṣlaḥa. tajahhaza, “to get oneself ready” (Form V), its shadda the print's own. li-al-safari, “for the journey”: li- of purpose.

sentences.t: فَمَا مَضَى ثَلٰثَةُ أَيَّامٍ حَتَّى قَضَى مَصَالِحَهُ وَخَرَجَ مُسَافِرًا إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā maḍā thalāthatu ayyāmin ḥattā qaḍā maṣāliḥahu wa-kharaja musāfiran ilā al-Baṣrati
sentences.l: And not had-passed three days until he-had-settled his-affairs and gone-out travelling to Basra.
sentences.i: Before three days had passed he had settled his affairs and set out on his journey to Basra.
sentences.n: mā … ḥattā, “not … until”: three days had not passed before he was done. maḍā is masculine, its subject thalāthatu ayyāmin coming after it; ثلٰثة is printed with its dagger alif. musāfiran, “travelling”, an accusative that says in what state he went out.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَ صَاحِبُهُ بَعْدَ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ لِيَزُورَهُ فَلَمْ يَجِدْةُ
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾa ṣāḥibuhu baʿda thalāthati ayyāmin li-yazūrahu fa-lam yajidhu
sentences.l: And his-companion came after three days to visit-him, and he-did-not find-him
sentences.i: Three days later his friend came to visit him, and did not find him
sentences.n: li-yazūrahu, “in order to visit him”: li- of purpose with a subjunctive verb. lam yajid, “he did not find”, jussive after lam. The print spells the pronoun -hu, “him”, with ة (يجدة), its habit.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَ عَنْهُ جِيرَانَهُ فَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّهُ تَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ مِنْ مُدَّةِ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ لِأَنَّ لَهُ مُعَامَلَاتٍ عِنْدَ تُجَّارِهَا فَذَهَبَ لِيُطَالِبَ أَرْبَابَ الدُّيُونِ وَعَنْ قَرِيبٍ يَأْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala ʿanhu jīrānahu fa-qālū lahu innahu tawajjaha ilā al-Baṣrati min muddati thalāthati ayyāmin li-anna lahu muʿāmalātin ʿinda tujjārihā fa-dhahaba li-yuṭāliba arbāba al-duyūni wa-ʿan qarībin yaʾtī
sentences.l: And he-asked about-him his-neighbours, and they-said to-him: He has-set-out for Basra, from a-span of three days, because to-him (are) dealings with its-merchants; so he-went to-demand-payment (of) the masters of the debts, and in a-short (while) he-comes.
sentences.i: He asked the neighbours about him, and they told him, “He left for Basra three days ago. He has dealings with the merchants there, and he has gone to call in what is owed him; he will be back before long.”
sentences.n: innahu, “he (has)”: after qāla the reported words open with inna, not anna. min muddati thalāthati ayyāmin, “from a span of three days”, is “three days ago”. li-anna lahu muʿāmalātin, “because to him are dealings”, is “because he has dealings”: lahu is the predicate, put first, and muʿāmalāt is accusative after anna. The -hā of tujjārihā, “its merchants”, is Basra; the shadda of تجّارها is the print's own. ṭālaba, Form III, “to press for payment”, with li- of purpose: li-yuṭāliba, “to press”. arbāb al-duyūn, “the masters of the debts”, would usually be the creditors, but here the sense needs the people who owe Abū al-Ḥasan money; the phrase is loose. ʿan qarībin, “before long”. yaʾtī, the present for the near future; its hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَاحْتَارَ الرَّجُلُ فِي أَمْرِةِ وَصَارَ لَا يَدْرِي أَيْنَ يَذْهَبُ وَقَالَ يَا لَيْتَنِي لَمْ أُفَارِقْ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-iḥtāra al-rajulu fī amrihi wa-ṣāra lā yadrī ayna yadhhabu wa-qāla yā laytanī lam ufāriq Abā al-Ḥasani
sentences.l: And the man became-perplexed in his-affair, and he-came-to not know where he-should-go, and he-said: O would-that-I had not parted-from Abū al-Ḥasan!
sentences.i: The man did not know what to do; he had no idea where to turn, and he said, “If only I had never left Abū al-Ḥasan's side!”
sentences.n: iḥtāra, “to be perplexed” (Form VIII of ḥāra). The print writes the pronoun of amrihi, “his affair”, with ة (امرة), its habit. ṣāra lā yadrī, “he came to not know”: ṣāra with an imperfect is “he was now …”. yā laytanī, “O would that I”, with lam and the jussive ufāriq (Form III), wishes something had not happened. Abā is the accusative of abū, as object of ufāriq.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَبَّرَ حِيلَةً يَتَوَصَّلُ بِهَا إِلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَقَصَدَ دَارَةُ وَقَالَ لِبَعْضِ غِلْمَانِهِ اسْتَأْذِنْ لِي سَيِّدَكَ لِأَ دْخُلَ أُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma dabbara ḥīlatan yatawaṣṣalu bihā ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-qaṣada dārahu wa-qāla li-baʿḍi ghilmānihi istaʾdhin lī sayyidaka li-adkhula usallimu ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then he-contrived a-device (that) he-might-make-his-way by-it to ʿAlī son of Bakkār; and he-made-for his-house and said to one of his-pages: Ask-leave for-me (of) your-master, that-I-may-enter (and) greet him.
sentences.i: Then he thought of a way to reach ʿAlī ibn Bakkār. He went to his house and said to one of the pages, “Ask your master's leave for me to come in and pay my respects.”
sentences.n: dabbara ḥīlatan, “to contrive a device” (Form II); the shadda of دبّر is the print's own. yatawaṣṣalu bihā ilā, “by which he might make his way to” (Form V of waṣala): a clause describing ḥīlatan with no relative word, the -hā of bihā pointing back to it. The print writes the pronoun of dārahu, “his house”, with ة (دارة). ghilmān is the plural of ghulām, “page, serving boy”. istaʾdhin lī sayyidaka, “ask your master's leave for me”: istaʾdhana, Form X, “to ask permission”, takes the person asked as its object; its hamza is the print's own. The print splits li-adkhula, “that I may enter”, into two words, لا دخل: the lām of purpose with the alif of the verb's prefix, and then the rest; read together they make one word, and the spacing is kept. usallimu ʿalayhi, “(and) greet him”, follows with no “and”; the shadda of اسلّم is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ الْغُلَامُ وَأَخْبَرَ سَيِّدَةُ بِهِ ثُمَّ عَادَ إِلَيْهِ وَأَذِنَ لَهُ فِى الدُّخُولِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala al-ghulāmu wa-akhbara sayyidahu bihi thumma ʿāda ilayhi wa-adhina lahu fī al-dukhūli
sentences.l: And the page went-in and informed his-master of-him; then he-returned to-him and gave-leave to-him in the entering.
sentences.i: The page went in and told his master about him, then came back and gave him leave to enter.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, “to inform someone of”: the verb chooses bi- for the news, here the visitor himself. The print writes sayyidahu, “his master”, with ة (سيدة); spelled so, it could be read sayyida, “lady”, but the sense settles it. adhina li- … fī, “to give someone leave for”: li- marks the one permitted, fī the thing permitted (in Night 158 the same verb took bi-). fī is printed فى, with ى.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ فَوَجَدَةُ مُلْقًى عَلَى الْوِسَادَةِ فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ وَرَحَّبَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala ʿalayhi fa-wajadahu mulqan ʿalā al-wisādati fa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhi al-salāma wa-raḥḥaba bihi
sentences.l: And he-went-in upon-him and found-him thrown-down on the cushion; and he-greeted him, and he-returned to-him the greeting and welcomed him.
sentences.i: He went in to him and found him lying limp on his cushion. He greeted him, and ʿAlī returned the greeting and bade him welcome.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”: the verb chooses ʿalā for the person visited. The print writes wajadahu, “he found him”, with ة (فوجدة). mulqan, “thrown down, lying”, passive participle of alqā (Form IV), accusative: it says in what state he was found. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”; the shadda of فسلّم is the print's own. radda ʿalayhi al-salāma, “returned the greeting to him”. raḥḥaba bi-, “to welcome” (Form II), takes bi- for the guest.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اعْتَذَرَ لَهُ ذَلِكَ الشَّابُّ فِي تَخَلُّفِهِ عَنْهُ تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةَ
sentences.tr: thumma iʿtadhara lahu dhālika al-shābbu fī takhallufihi ʿanhu tilka al-muddata
sentences.l: Then that young-man excused-himself to-him for his-staying-away from-him that period.
sentences.i: Then the young man apologised for having stayed away from him all that while.
sentences.n: The young man is the visitor, Abū al-Ḥasan's friend, who had not called on ʿAlī in his illness. iʿtadhara li- … fī, “to apologise to someone for” (Form VIII of ʿadhara): li- marks the one apologised to, fī the fault. takhalluf ʿan, “staying behind from, failing to come to”, verbal noun of Form V. tilka al-muddata, “that period”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي إِنَّ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ صَدَاقَةً وَإِنِّي كُنْتُ أُوَدِّعُهُ أَسْرَارِى وَلَا أَنْقَطِعُ عَنْهُ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu yā sayyidī inna baynī wa-bayna Abī al-Ḥasani ṣadāqatan wa-innī kuntu uwaddiʿuhu asrārī wa-lā anqaṭiʿu ʿanhu sāʿatan
sentences.l: Then he-said to-him: O my-master, between-me and between Abū al-Ḥasan (is) friendship, and I used-to entrust-him (with) my-secrets, and not cut-myself-off from-him an-hour.
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Sir, Abū al-Ḥasan and I are friends. I used to confide all my secrets to him, and I was never away from him for an hour.
sentences.n: inna baynī wa-bayna Abī al-Ḥasani ṣadāqatan, “between me and between Abū al-Ḥasan is friendship”: Arabic repeats bayn with each party; the phrase in front is the predicate, and ṣadāqatan is accusative after inna. kuntu with an imperfect, “I used to”, and it carries on over lā anqaṭiʿu, “I would not cut myself off” (Form VII). The shadda of اودّعه, the print's own, makes the verb Form II, waddaʿa, whose usual sense is “to bid farewell”; the sense here, “to entrust with”, belongs to Form IV, awdaʿa. The reading here keeps the print's shadda and takes the sense the sentence needs; the shadda may be a slip. It takes two objects, the person (-hu) and the thing (asrārī, “my secrets”, which the print ends with ى, اسرارى). The shadda of وانّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَغِبْتُ فِي بَعْضِ الْمَصَالِحِ مَعَ جَمَاعَةٍ مِنْ رُفَقَائِي مُدَّةَ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ ثُمَّ جِئْتُ إِلَيْهِ فَوَجَدْتُ دُكَّانَهُ مَقْفُولَةً فَسَأَلْتُ عَنْهُ الْجِيرَانَ فَقَالُوا إِنَّهُ تَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ghibtu fī baʿḍi al-maṣāliḥi maʿa jamāʿatin min rufaqāʾī muddata thalāthati ayyāmin thumma jiʾtu ilayhi fa-wajadtu dukkānahu maqfūlatan fa-saʾaltu ʿanhu al-jīrāna fa-qālū innahu tawajjaha ilā al-Baṣrati
sentences.l: And I-was-away on some (of) the affairs with a-party of my-companions a-span of three days; then I-came to-him and found his-shop locked; and I-asked about-him the neighbours, and they-said: He has-set-out for Basra.
sentences.i: I was away on some business with a party of my companions for three days, and when I came back to him I found his shop locked up. I asked the neighbours about him, and they said he had gone to Basra.
sentences.n: The ḍamma of فغبتُ is the print's own. fī baʿḍi al-maṣāliḥi, “on some business”: maṣāliḥ, plural of maṣlaḥa, “an affair, a matter in hand”. rufaqāʾ, plural of rafīq, “companion”. muddata, “for the span of”, accusative of time. maqfūla, “locked” (passive participle of qafala), is feminine: dukkān, “shop”, is treated as feminine again, as in Night 158. The shadda of دكّانه, and the hamzas of رفقائي, جئت and فسألت, are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ لَهُ صَدِيقًا أَوْفَى مِنْكَ فَبِاللَّهِ عَرِّفْنِي خَبَرَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam aʿlam lahu ṣadīqan awfā minka fa-bi-Allāhi ʿarrifnī khabarahu
sentences.l: And I-have-not known for-him a-friend more-faithful than-you; so by-God, make-me-know his-news.
sentences.i: I know of no friend of his more faithful than you; so, by God, tell me what has become of him.”
sentences.n: lam aʿlam lahu ṣadīqan, “I have not known for him a friend”, i.e. “I know of no friend of his”. awfā, “more faithful”, elative of wafiyy; min marks what is compared, “than you”. fa-bi-Allāhi, “so by God”: bi- of the oath, used to plead. ʿarrafa, Form II, “to make known”, takes two objects, the person (-nī, “me”) and the thing (khabarahu, “his news”).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ كَلَامَهُ تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنُهُ وَاضْطَرَبَ وَقَالَ لَمْ أَسْمَعْ قَبْلَ هَذَا الْيَوْمِ خَبَرَ سَفَرِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ الْأَمْرُ كَمَا ذَكَرْتَ فَقَدْ حَصَلَ لِيَ التَّعَبُ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin kalāmahu taghayyara lawnuhu wa-iḍṭaraba wa-qāla lam asmaʿ qabla hādhā al-yawmi khabara safarihi wa-in kāna al-amru ka-mā dhakarta fa-qad ḥaṣala liya al-taʿabu wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār heard his-speech, his-colour changed and he-was-shaken, and he-said: I-have-not heard before this day (the) news of his-journey; and if the matter is as you-mentioned, then the weariness has-come to-me. And he-recited, saying:
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār heard what he said, his colour changed and he was shaken. “I had heard nothing of his journey before today,” he said, “and if things are as you say, then my troubles are upon me.” And he recited:
sentences.n: taghayyara lawnuhu, “his colour changed” (Form V); the shadda of تغيّر is the print's own. iḍṭaraba, “to be agitated, to tremble” (Form VIII of ḍaraba; the t of the form becomes ṭ after ḍ). in kāna … fa-qad, “if it is … then”: fa- with qad brings in the answer to the condition. ka-mā dhakarta, “as you mentioned”: ka-, “like”, + mā, “what”. ḥaṣala li-, “to come to, befall someone”; al-taʿab, “weariness, toil”, here his distress. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”: the usual way of bringing in verse.

sentences.t:
قَدْ كُنْتُ اَبْكِي عَلَى مَا فَاتَ مِنْ فَرَحٍ * وَاَهْلُ وُدِّي جَمِيْعًا غَيْرُ اَشْتَاتِ
وَالْيَوْمَ فَرَّقَ مَا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُمْ * دَهْرِي فَاَبْكِي عَلَى اَهْلِ الْمَوَدَّاتِ
sentences.tr:
qad kuntu abkī ʿalā mā fāta min faraḥin * wa-ahlu wuddī jamīʿan ghayru ashtāti
wa-al-yawma farraqa mā baynī wa-baynahum * dahrī fa-abkī ʿalā ahli al-mawaddāti
sentences.l:
I used-to weep over what had-passed of joy, * while the people of my-love, all-together, (were) not scattered;
And today has-parted what (is) between-me and-between-them * my-time, so I-weep over the people of the affections.
sentences.i:
Once I wept for the joys that had slipped away, while those I loved were all still gathered close;
Now fate has set a gulf between me and them, and I weep for the friends I love.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ. The pointing is the print's own. It writes the hamza of abkī and ahl as a bare alif with fatḥa (اَبْكِي, وَاَهْلُ, اَشْتَاتِ), and sets a sukūn on the long ī of jamīʿan (جَمِيْعًا), a habit of its verse pointing. wa-ahlu wuddī …, “while my loved ones …”: a circumstantial clause with wa-. ashtāt, “scattered, apart”, plural of shatt; ghayru ashtāti, “not scattered”. wudd and mawadda both mean “affection, love”; ahl al-mawaddāt, “the people of the affections”, are his friends. In the second line the subject, dahrī, “my time, my fortune”, waits until after the caesura: “today my fortune has parted what was between me and them”. Then he wept for lost joy among his friends; now he weeps for the friends themselves. The rhyme is -āti.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلِيًّا بْنَ بَكَّارٍ أَطْرَقَ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ يَتَفَكَّرُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna ʿAliyyan ibna Bakkārin aṭraqa raʾsahu ilā al-arḍi yatafakkaru
sentences.l: Then ʿAlī son of Bakkār lowered his-head to the ground, reflecting.
sentences.i: Then ʿAlī ibn Bakkār bowed his head towards the ground, lost in thought.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was so) that”, is the narrator's way of starting a new step; the noun after inna is accusative, and the print writes the -an of ʿAliyyan with its alif (عليا). Classical usage drops the -n when ibn stands between two names (ʿAliyya bna Bakkārin); the alif shows the print reading it with the -n kept. aṭraqa, Form IV, “to bow the head in silence”. yatafakkaru, “reflecting” (Form V), an imperfect describing his state; its shadda is the print's own, and so is the hamza of رأسه.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ إِلَى خَادِمٍ لَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ امْضِ إِلَى دَارِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ وَاسْأَلْ عَنْهُ هَلْ هُوَ مُقِيمٌ أَوْ مُسَافِرٌ فَإِنْ قَالُوا سَافَرَ فَاسْأَلْ إِلَى أَيِّ جِهَةٍ تَوَجَّهَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda sāʿatin rafaʿa raʾsahu ilā khādimin lahu wa-qāla lahu imḍi ilā dāri Abī al-Ḥasani wa-isʾal ʿanhu hal huwa muqīmun aw musāfirun fa-in qālū sāfara fa-isʾal ilā ayyi jihatin tawajjaha
sentences.l: And after an-hour he-raised his-head to a-servant of-his and said to-him: Go to the house of Abū al-Ḥasan and ask about-him: is he staying or travelling? And if they-say (he) has-travelled, then ask to which quarter he-set-out.
sentences.i: After a while he raised his head, turned to one of his servants and said, “Go to Abū al-Ḥasan's house and ask after him: is he at home or away? If they say he has gone on a journey, ask where he went.”
sentences.n: sāʿa, “an hour”, is any short while. rafaʿa raʾsahu ilā, “he raised his head to”: he looks up towards the servant. khādimin lahu, “a servant of his”. imḍi, “go!”, imperative of maḍā. muqīm, “staying, at home”, against musāfir, “travelling, away”. fa-in qālū sāfara, “and if they say, (he) has travelled”: a past verb after in. ilā ayyi jihatin, “to which quarter”; the shadda of ايّ is the print's own, and so are the hamzas of رأسه, واسأل and فاسأل.

sentences.t: فَمَضَي الْغُلَامُ وَغَابَ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَ إِلَى سَيِّدِهِ وَقَالَ إِنِّي لَمَّا سَأَلْتُ عَنْ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ أَخْبَرَنِي أَهْلُهُ أَنَّهُ سَافَرَ إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-maḍā al-ghulāmu wa-ghāba sāʿatan thumma aqbala ilā sayyidihi wa-qāla innī lammā saʾaltu ʿan Abī al-Ḥasani akhbaranī ahluhu annahu sāfara ilā al-Baṣrati
sentences.l: And the page went-off and was-away an-hour; then he-came to his-master and said: I, when I-asked about Abū al-Ḥasan, his-people informed-me that he had-travelled to Basra.
sentences.i: The page went off and was gone a while; then he came back to his master and said, “When I asked after Abū al-Ḥasan, his household told me he had gone to Basra.
sentences.n: The print writes maḍā with a dotted yāʾ (فمضي) where Classical spelling has alif maqṣūra (مضى). ʿAlī sent a khādim, “servant”, and the narrator now calls him al-ghulām, “the page”: both words are used of the same boy. aqbala ilā, “to come towards” (Form IV). innī lammā saʾaltu …, “I, when I asked …”: the speaker puts himself first with innī and then lets the sentence run its own way, a loose spoken build. ahluhu, “his people”, his household; the verb before it, akhbaranī, is singular, as a verb that comes first usually is. The hamza of سألت is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ وَجَدْتُ جَارِيَةً وَاقِفَةً عَلَى الْبَابِ فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي عَرَفَتْنِي وَلَمْ أَعْرِفْهَا وَقَالَتْ لِي هَلْ أَنْتَ غُلَامُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin wajadtu jāriyatan wāqifatan ʿalā al-bābi fa-lammā raʾatnī ʿarafatnī wa-lam aʿrifhā wa-qālat lī hal anta ghulāmu ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: But I-found a-slave-girl standing at the door; and when she-saw-me she-knew-me, and I-did-not know-her, and she-said to-me: Are you the page of ʿAlī son of Bakkār?
sentences.i: But I found a slave-girl standing at the door. When she saw me she knew me, though I did not know her, and she said to me, ‘Are you ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's page?’
sentences.n: wa-lākin, “but”: the light form lākin, which can take a verb straight after it. wāqifatan, “standing”, accusative, describing jāriyatan. raʾatnī, “she saw me”; the hamza is the print's own. wa-lam aʿrifhā, “and I did not know her”, a circumstantial clause: “though I did not know her”. hal is the plain question word, “is it that …?”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا نَعَمْ فَقَالَتْ إِنَّ مَعِي رِسَالَةً إِلَيْهِ مِنْ عِنْدِ أَعَزِّ النَّاسِ عَلَيْهِ فَجَاءَتْ مَعِي وَهِيَ وَاقِفَةٌ عَلَى الْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā naʿam fa-qālat inna maʿī risālatan ilayhi min ʿindi aʿazzi al-nāsi ʿalayhi fa-jāʾat maʿī wa-hiya wāqifatun ʿalā al-bābi
sentences.l: And I-said to-her: Yes. And she-said: With-me (is) a-message to-him from (the) side of the dearest of the people to-him. And she-came with-me, and she (is) standing at the door.
sentences.i: ‘Yes,’ I told her, and she said, ‘I have a message for him from the one he holds dearest in all the world.’ So she came with me, and she is standing at the door now.”
sentences.n: inna maʿī risālatan, “with me is a message”: maʿī, put first, is the predicate, and risālatan is accusative after inna. min ʿindi, “from beside”, simply “from”. aʿazzu al-nāsi ʿalayhi, “the dearest of people to him”: aʿazz is the elative of ʿazīz, “dear”, and ʿalā marks the one to whom someone is dear. It is a veiled way of naming Shams al-Nahār. wa-hiya wāqifatun, “and she is standing”: a circumstantial clause with wa-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ أَدْخِلْهَا فَطَلَعَ الْغُلَامُ إِلَيْهَا وَأَدْخَلَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin adkhilhā fa-ṭalaʿa al-ghulāmu ilayhā wa-adkhalahā
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: Make-her-enter. And the page went-out to-her and made-her-enter.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “Bring her in.” The page went out to her and brought her in.
sentences.n: adkhilhā, “bring her in”, singular imperative of Form IV adkhala: this time the order goes to the page alone (in Night 158 it was the plural adkhilūhā). ṭalaʿa, “to go up, come out”: here the page goes out to the girl at the door.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي عِنْدَ ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ فَوَجَدَهَا ظَرِيفَةً
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-rajulu alladhī ʿinda ibni Bakkārin ilā al-jāriyati fa-wajadahā ẓarīfatan
sentences.l: And the man who (was) with Ibn Bakkār looked at the slave-girl and found-her graceful.
sentences.i: The man who was sitting with Ibn Bakkār looked at the girl and found her charming.
sentences.n: al-rajul, “the man”, is Abū al-Ḥasan's friend, still at ʿAlī's side. ʿAlī is now called Ibn Bakkār, by his father's name alone, and the print writes ابن with its alif. naẓara ilā, “to look at”: the verb chooses ilā. ẓarīfa, “graceful, elegant, charming”, accusative as the second object of wajada.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ تَقَدَّمَتْ عِنْدَ ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata taqaddamat ʿinda ibni Bakkārin wa-sallamat ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl came-forward to Ibn Bakkār and greeted him.
sentences.i: Then the girl came forward to Ibn Bakkār and greeted him.
sentences.n: taqaddama, “to step forward” (Form V), here with ʿinda, “at, beside”, where Classical would say ilā: she comes up to where he lies.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept.
